title: vendorfiles program registry
description: Programs `vendor add <name>` can install without being told a repository or its asset names. Describes version 1 of the format; a later version bumps the number and this file with it.

version.description: Schema version. A vendor that does not understand the number refuses the file rather than misreading it.

programs.description: Programs by canonical name, which is also the config key `add` writes.

aliases.description: Other names that resolve here. Canonical names win, so an alias can never redirect an existing name.

repository.description: The GitHub repository releases come from. The same shape `vendor add <url>` takes, `www.` and plain `http` included.

releaseRegex.description: Which tags count, for a repository publishing several trains of releases. `bitwarden/sdk` tags `bws-v2.1.0` alongside `rust-v2.1.0`, and only the first carries binaries.

path.description: A file in the repository rather than a release asset. Mutually exclusive with `asset`, `member` and `targets`.

hashVersionFile.description: Track a repository file by commit rather than by tag. Only `path` entries have a commit to track, so `true` needs one.

asset.description: The asset pattern shared by every target, for projects naming assets by target triple. Placeholders: {release}, {version}, {target}, {ext}, {exe}.

as.description: The name to save it under, when the basename is not the command you would type: `ox-macos` becomes `ox`.

targets.description: What to fetch per host, keyed `{os}-{arch}` exactly as Rust reports them.

With no shared `asset` there is no pattern for a triple to substitute into, so every host has to name its assets outright - and each names its own `member`, the shared one having no asset to point into.

then.description: `true` tracks the first file's commit, which only a repository `path` has. A release asset would send the lookup after a path containing `{release}/`.
More than one member means each file lands under its own name, so there is no single file for `as` to rename.

target.description: Either the target triple to substitute into the shared patterns, or the assets named outright.

spelledOut.description: One asset named outright, or the several a host needs together - an archive holding the program, say, beside a loose file it reads.

asset.description: The release asset, including the `{release}/` prefix.

as.description: The name to save it under.

then.description: More than one member means each file lands under its own name, so there is no single file for `as` to rename.

member.description: What to take out of the asset. One path is the executable, saved under its basename, which `as` may rename. A list is a layout every file of which is written out as it stands: `herdr.exe` loads the `conpty/` directory shipped beside it, and flattening would collide `conpty/x64/OpenConsole.exe` with the `arm64` build of the same name. A map is that same layout with the destinations spelled out, for an archive that buries what you want: `x64/programz.exe` under the name `program.exe`.
